::: {.callout-note appearance="simple"}
**The forward arrow, reversed.** Everywhere else on this site Plexus runs
*forward*: a small typed **spec** (sets, fields, operators, a schedule) is
interpreted by a generic engine into a simulation,
$\text{spec}\to\text{engine}\to\text{trajectory}$. This page inverts that arrow.
Given **only a simulation** — the cell positions and the chemical field over time
— we recover the eight-number spec that generated it. It is the first inverse
result built directly on the Plexus operators, and it works because those
operators are explicit *and* differentiable.
:::

## From the forward model to its inverse

The [slime](index.qmd#what-it-looks-like) spec is **eight continuous numbers**: four on the
field side (`deposit.amount`, `diffuse.rate`, `decay.rate`, `sense.cross`) and
four per-cell motion parameters (`move_speed`, `turn_speed`, `sensor_angle`,
`sensor_dist`). The registered operators make every cell deposit into a chemical
field, sense that field at three forward sensors, turn toward the strongest
reading, and advance; the field meanwhile diffuses and decays. From a
uniform-random start the population condenses into a filament network. The
**inverse** problem is $\text{trajectory}\to\text{spec}$: identify those eight
constants from the observed evolution alone.

## Method

**What is learned, and from what.** The only learnables are the **eight numbers of
the spec** — the constants of the operators. What is *given* is one observed
simulation: the **cell positions and the chemical field at each recorded time**.
Recovery adjusts those eight numbers — by gradient descent on the differentiable
operators, or by a black-box UCB search — until a fresh run reproduces the observed
trajectory. The architecture is fixed; only the constants of a *known* generative
law are fit.

**The parameters split by what couples to what.** In the Plexus language the slime
is a composition of typed operators, and its eight numbers group by the *kind* of
coupling they parameterise:

- **Particle ↔ field — `Exchange`.** `deposit` pushes each cell's mass into the
  chemical field (`deposit.amount`); `sense` pulls the field back at three forward
  sensors and steers up it (`sensor_angle`, `sensor_dist`, `turn_speed`,
  `move_speed`, and the inter-type weight `cross`). These are the *only* operators
  that move information between the discrete cells and the continuous field.
- **Field ↔ field — within the field.** `diffuse` couples each field cell to its
  neighbours (`diffuse.rate`) and `decay` relaxes each cell toward zero
  (`decay.rate`); with several types the field carries one channel per type and
  `cross` mixes them. This half is spatially local and **linear** in its parameters.
- **Particle ↔ particle — none, by construction.** The single-type slime has *no*
  direct cell–cell operator: cells influence each other *only through the field*
  they share (deposit → diffuse → sense). There is nothing to identify at this
  level — a genuine `Lateral` neighbour law (boids, adhesion) would simply be fit
  from the same position loss below, if the model contained one.

**How each coupling is recovered.** Because the field half is linear, a single
**teacher-forced** step $\text{field}_t\to\text{field}_{t+1}$ recovers
`deposit.amount`, `diffuse.rate` and `decay.rate` to $\sim\!10^{-3}$, plus
`move_speed` from the displacement — about **224× more accurate** than the black-box
UCB baseline, which left `diffuse.rate` in the wrong half of its range. The
particle-↔-field **sensing** parameters are recovered by placing the loss **directly
on the predicted particle positions** (free-run `sense`→`glide`, match where the
cells are), which removes an earlier `sensor_angle` bias from reconstructing a
heading as $\operatorname{atan2}$ of the displacement; a short step beats a long
recurrent rollout, which accumulates chaos. The inter-type `cross` cannot be pinned
from one type — it is *held* at ground truth — but becomes identifiable once several
types make it drive the dynamics, more sharply as the type count grows.

**Engine-exact operators.** Every operator is mirrored by one differentiable
`nn.Module` whose parameters are tensors and whose output is checked against the
real engine (`deposit`, `diffuse`, `decay`, `glide` match to $\le 10^{-7}$);
`sense` is the one non-differentiable operator — a hard three-way branch plus a
random turn — so it is replaced by a smooth mixture surrogate. A fit on these
modules is a fit on the *real* dynamics, and likelihood *profiles* (scanning one
parameter with the rest fixed) are the diagnostic that told a "biased objective"
apart from a "genuinely unidentifiable" one.

## Results: do we recover the parameters?

The recovery is explicit, parameter by parameter, with values in the unit cube
$u\in[0,1]$. For a single type the
field parameters and `move_speed` are exact; `turn_speed`, `sensor_angle` and
`sensor_dist` recover to a few percent; `cross` is *held* because a single type
cannot constrain it. For **four types every parameter including `cross` is
recovered** (`cross` u-error $0.008$ at four types, $0.012$ at two). Across four
random single-type targets the `sensor_angle` u-error is
$0.015\,/\,0.158\,/\,0.092\,/\,0.051$ — the spread tracks how much lateral field
structure each target presents to the sensors.


The recovered spec does not match the target frame-for-frame — the process is
stochastic — but produces the **same topology**: the same filament network, loop
density and length scale.

![Ground truth vs the best recovery (8D position-loss) over time (*t* = 0 → 200): the top two rows are the **agents** (ground truth and a run from the recovered eight-number spec), the bottom two the same runs drawn as the **chemical field** they deposit. Both start from spatial noise and condense tick by tick into a filament network — a *written* generative process, not a learned one. Because the dynamics are stochastic the recovered run never matches frame-for-frame; what it reproduces is the target's **topology** (branch density, loop statistics, length scale), the invariant the inverse problem solves for.](figures/fig_inverse_evolution.png){fig-align="center"}

## Three observations

#### 1. The rollout is a written generative process.

The time-lapse looks like a generative diffusion model: each rollout starts from
spatial **noise** — uniformly random cell positions and an empty field — and tick
by tick condenses that noise into a definite morphology, a path from noise to a
sample on the data manifold. The decisive difference is that the generative law is
**not** a learned black box: the transition kernel $x_{t+1}=\Phi(x_t)$ is the
explicitly written calculus of operators (`deposit`, `diffuse`, `decay`, `sense`,
`advance`), and the prior it samples from is fixed by $\sim\!8$ interpretable
constants. The inverse problem is therefore not "invert a neural sampler" but
"identify the few physical constants of a *known* generative law" — which is
exactly why a handful of gradient steps suffice where amortizing a diffusion prior
would not. The stochasticity (the random seed, the random turn in `sense`) plays
the role of the diffusion noise schedule: any single rollout is one sample,
reproducible only in distribution, never pixel-for-pixel.

#### 2. Parameters encode a topology, not a configuration.

This reframes what "recovering the spec" means. Two rollouts of the *same* spec
under different seeds are never identical point-for-point, yet they are the same
object topologically — the same kind of filament web, with the same branch
density, loop statistics and characteristic length. The parameters do not encode a
particular configuration; they encode a **topology**, equivalently a *dynamical
regime* — the attractor onto which the operator flow condenses noise. Different
parameter regions encode qualitatively different topologies (a space-filling
network vs. isolated clusters vs. a near-lattice), separated by bifurcations of
the operator dynamics. So the inverse map is really *observed topology* → *the
dynamical law whose attractor has that topology*, and the per-parameter
identifiability findings are the precise statement that some topological features
pin some parameters (lateral field structure pins `sensor_angle`; multi-channel
structure pins `cross`) while leaving others free. Recovering the spec is
recovering the **generator** of a topology, not the topology itself — which is the
version of the problem that is both well posed and useful.

#### 3. Why the match is topological, not pointwise.

Because the success criterion is distributional, the correct loss must be too. A
pointwise position loss works only on a short, pre-chaotic horizon; over long
horizons the same spec decorrelates from itself, and the only stable signal is the
topology — which is why behaviour-level, permutation-invariant comparisons (and
the per-frame, short-horizon position loss used here) succeed where long pointwise
rollouts fail. The encoded "dynamics/topology" is thus the invariant the inverse
problem is actually solving for.

::: {.callout-tip appearance="simple"}
**Why this matters for Plexus.** The same explicit, differentiable primitives that
make a behaviour "a new sentence in the language" also make its inverse tractable:
the same spec serves prediction, **inverse inference**, and — next — the
optimization of biological designs. A full static write-up is in
[`prototype/inverse_slime/inverse_slime.pdf`](prototype/inverse_slime/inverse_slime.pdf).
:::

## Gallery: all ground-truth-vs-recovery panels

The panels below reproduce every visual page of the report: the showcase
single-type target (method comparison), three further single-type targets, and
the two-type and four-type cases (cells coloured by type; the multi-channel field
shown as a per-species colour composite). In every panel the **top row is ground
truth** and the rows below are recoveries; columns are time.

### Showcase single-type target

The showcase target is shown four ways along two axes: **what is drawn** — the cells/agents or the chemical field they deposit — and **which method** — the two best recoveries (8D gradient-descent) or the weaker baselines (4D gradient-descent, black-box search). In every montage the top row is the ground-truth simulation, the rows beneath are runs from the recovered parameters, and columns are time (*t* = 0 → 200).

![**Cells — best methods.** Top row ground truth; below it the two strongest recoveries, both full eight-parameter gradient-descent fits that differ only in the loss. **8D position-loss** puts the loss on the predicted particle positions (matching where the cells are), which removes the `sensor_angle` bias and makes it the best; **8D heading-loss** matches a reconstructed heading instead and pushes `sensor_angle` too high. Reading left to right, both condense into the same filament morphology as the target — a topological match, not a frame-for-frame one.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_00.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Chemical field — best methods.** The same three runs, drawn as the **chemical trail field** rather than the agents. The field is the linear, teacher-forced half of the problem, so a single field step recovers `deposit`, `diffuse` and `decay` to ~10⁻³ and both recoveries reproduce the target field almost exactly. That tight field match is *why* the harder sensing parameters can be identified from the agents at all.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_01.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Cells — baselines.** Ground truth on top, with two deliberately weaker methods below. **4D gradient-descent (field + move)** fits only the field parameters plus `move_speed`, leaving the three sensing parameters unconstrained; **UCB black-box search** uses no gradients, left `diffuse.rate` in the wrong half of its range, and is about **224× less accurate**. As time advances these baselines drift off the target network where the best 8D fits stay locked on.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_02.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Chemical field — baselines.** The same two baseline recoveries drawn as the deposited field, ground truth on top. Because the field parameters are the most identifiable, even these weaker methods reproduce the broad trail early on. But the black-box search's misplaced `diffuse.rate` shows up as a field that spreads too fast or slow, coarsening away from the target over time.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_03.png){fig-align="center"}

### Three further single-type targets

Three more random single-type targets, each recovered with the best method (8D position-loss) and shown as both cells and chemical field. Same layout as above — top row ground truth, bottom row the recovered run, columns are time (*t* = 0 → 200). Recovery quality varies with the target: `sensor_angle` is pinned when the target offers rich lateral field structure and left looser when it does not (its unit-cube error ranged 0.015–0.158 across four such targets).

![**Target 1 — cells.** Ground truth (top) vs the 8D position-loss recovery (bottom). The field parameters and `move_speed` recover exactly and the sensing parameters to a few percent, so the recovered run condenses into the same filament network. As everywhere here the match is topological — branch density and length scale — not frame-for-frame.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_04.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Target 1 — chemical field.** The same two runs drawn as the deposited trail field. Because the field parameters recover to ~10⁻³, the ground-truth and recovered fields are nearly indistinguishable at every timepoint.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_05.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Target 2 — cells.** A second random target, ground truth vs position-loss recovery. This one offers the sensors less lateral field structure, so its `sensor_angle` is among the least tightly pinned — yet the recovered network still reproduces the target's density and length scale. It shows the identifiability finding directly: what the topology doesn't constrain, the fit leaves loose.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_06.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Target 2 — chemical field.** The same runs as the trail field. Even for this harder target the field is an almost exact match, because the field half of the spec is the linear, well-identified one.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_07.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Target 3 — cells.** A third random target, ground truth vs position-loss recovery. The recovered spec matches the target topology across the full time course, with the sensing parameters recovering more tightly here than for Target 2.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_08.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Target 3 — chemical field.** The recovered field tracks the ground-truth field in structure at every timepoint. The two differ only by the stochastic seed, not by the fitted parameters.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_09.png){fig-align="center"}

### Two-type and four-type slime — `cross` now recovered

A single type cannot constrain the inter-type coupling `cross`, so above it is held at ground truth. With several types the field carries one channel per type and each cell reads a `cross`-weighted blend of its own channel and the total, so `cross` now drives the dynamics and becomes identifiable — more sharply as the type count grows (unit-cube error 0.012 at two types, 0.008 at four). These montages show the two- and four-type targets recovered in full: cells coloured by type, the multi-channel field as a per-species composite, ground truth on top and recovery below.

![**Two-type — cells.** Ground truth vs full recovery, cells coloured by type. With two channels present `cross` becomes identifiable (unit-cube error 0.012) and *every* parameter is recovered, not just the single-type-identifiable ones. The two types segregate into interleaved networks, which the recovered run reproduces over time.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_10.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Two-type — chemical field.** The two trail channels shown as a per-species colour composite. The recovered field reproduces the inter-type mixing that makes `cross` observable in the first place.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_11.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Four-type — cells.** Four types make `cross` the most sharply identifiable of all (unit-cube error 0.008), and the recovered spec reproduces the target down to that coupling. Cells are coloured by type, ground truth on top and recovery below; more channels give the fit more constraints, so accuracy improves with the type count.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_12.png){fig-align="center"}

![**Four-type — chemical field.** The four-channel field as a per-species colour composite, ground truth vs recovery. The matching per-species structure across the four channels is exactly what pins `cross` at four types.](figures/fig_inverse_gal_13.png){fig-align="center"}
